extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners; patent applicants and practitioners; public stakeholders commenting on §101 guidance
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for applying the Alice/Mayo two‑part framework (Steps 2A and 2B) to determine patent subject matter eligibility, including how to identify judicial exceptions, apply the markedly different characteristics analysis, evaluate whether additional elements amount to 'significantly more', and document a prima facie rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two‑part Alice/Mayo framework (Steps 2A and 2B)
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply the Supreme Court’s two‑part framework as Steps 2A and 2B: Step 2A—determine whether the claim is directed to a judicial exception (law of nature, natural phenomenon, or abstract idea); Step 2B—if so, determine whether the claim as a whole contains additional elements that amount to 'significantly more' than the exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use case law comparisons to identify exceptions in Step 2A; use the 'significantly more' inquiry in Step 2B to evaluate whether additional elements (individually and in combination) render the claim eligible. The framework already incorporates preemption concerns; follow the flowchart in the 2014 IEG and this Update.

rubrics_metrics.name: Markedly Different Characteristics (MDC) analysis in Step 2A
rubrics_metrics.description: For claims reciting nature‑based products, determine whether the recited product has 'markedly different characteristics' from what occurs in nature; if so, the claim is not directed to a 'product of nature' and may qualify as eligible at Step 2A.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: MDC is retained in Step 2A to provide (1) early eligibility for many claims, (2) an additional pathway to eligibility for product‑of‑nature exceptions, and (3) consistency across technologies. Examples (e.g., Chakrabarty, Myriad/cDNA, and Examples such as NBP‑2 pomelo juice) illustrate application. Do not move MDC to Step 2B.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider additional elements individually and in combination (Step 2B)
rubrics_metrics.description: In Step 2B, examiners must consider all additional claim elements both individually and in combination to determine whether the claim as a whole amounts to significantly more than the judicial exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if an element is generic (e.g., a generic computer component) and does not amount to significantly more on its own, it may do so in combination with other elements. Use examples (AI‑3, AI‑4, 21, 25) to see how combinations of generic components can perform non‑generic functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identifying abstract ideas by comparison to case law
rubrics_metrics.description: Because courts have not provided a single definition of 'abstract idea,' examiners should identify abstract ideas by comparing the claimed concept to concepts already held to be abstract in Supreme Court and Federal Circuit decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Associate claimed concepts with judicial descriptors derived from case law to avoid overbroad identification; ensure a claimed concept is not labeled abstract unless similar to at least one concept the courts have identified as an abstract idea. Newly discovered concepts can still be judicial exceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial descriptors for abstract ideas: 'fundamental economic practices'
rubrics_metrics.description: Concepts relating to the economy and commerce (agreements, contracts, legal obligations, business relations, financial transactions) are described as 'fundamental economic practices' and may be abstract.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples from case law include creating contractual relationships (buySAFE) and hedging/mitigating financial risk (Bilski, Alice Corp.). The term 'fundamental' is used to mean foundational/basic, not necessarily old.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial descriptors for abstract ideas: 'certain methods of organizing human activity'
rubrics_metrics.description: Concepts relating to interpersonal/intrapersonal activities — managing relationships or transactions between people, social activities, satisfying/avoiding legal obligations, advertising/marketing/sales, or managing human mental activity — can fall within this descriptor and may be abstract.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Not all methods of organizing human activity are abstract; the category is qualified as 'certain.' Case examples include buySAFE, Bilski, Alice, Dealertrack, Bancorp, Planet Bingo, Gametek, Accenture, and others. Use case comparisons to justify identification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial descriptors for abstract ideas: 'an idea "of itself"'
rubrics_metrics.description: Uninstantiated concepts, plans, schemes, or mental processes that can be performed in the human mind or with pen and paper are considered 'ideas of themselves' and may be abstract.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include mental processes of comparing or organizing information (Ambry, Myriad CAFC, Classen, Perkin‑Elmer, Grams, Cybersource, SmartGene). Note overlapping with other categories; use case law analogies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial descriptors for abstract ideas: 'mathematical relationships/formulas'
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematical concepts — algorithms, relationships, formulas, and calculations — are described as 'mathematical relationships/formulas' and may be judicial exceptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case examples: Benson, Flook, Mackay Radio, Diehr, Bilski, FuzzySharp, In re Maucorps, In re Grams, Freddie Mac, In re Abele. Courts have sometimes described mathematical concepts as laws of nature; rely on precedent when asserting this descriptor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples of computer functions considered well‑understood, routine, and conventional
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts have recognized certain generic computer functions as well‑understood, routine, and conventional when claimed in a merely generic manner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Listed examples include: performing repetitive calculations; receiving, processing, and storing data; electronically scanning or extracting data from a physical document (OCR); electronic recordkeeping; automating mental tasks; receiving or transmitting data over a network (e.g., Internet). Use these as benchmarks in Step 2B to determine whether additional elements are merely routine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prima facie case requirements for eligibility rejections
rubrics_metrics.description: An examiner meets the initial burden (prima facie case) by clearly articulating why a claim is not eligible: identify the judicial exception recited and why it is considered an exception, identify any additional elements, and explain why those elements do not amount to significantly more than the exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The rationale may rely on general knowledge in the art, case law precedent, applicant disclosure, or evidence. Training worksheets and sample rejections (Examples 5‑8) illustrate how to satisfy this burden. After the examiner meets the initial burden, the burden shifts to the applicant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of evidence and judicial notice in eligibility determinations
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts typically resolve eligibility as a question of law and have not required evidence to identify judicial exceptions; similarly, examiners may rely on judicial notice and their expertise in identifying routine, well‑understood elements in Step 2B.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although courts sometimes cited background documents as illustrative (e.g., Bilski and Alice), appellate courts did not treat those documents as evidence. Examiners should make a reasoned rationale in the record; a rejection should be made only if an examiner can readily conclude (based on expertise and precedent) that additional elements are merely well‑understood, routine, and conventional. If elements are beyond those recognized as routine, they will likely amount to significantly more.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of preemption in the eligibility analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Preemption is the underlying concern driving judicial exceptions, but is not a stand‑alone test; preemption considerations are embedded in the two‑part Alice/Mayo framework used in Steps 2A and 2B.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A claim that preempts a basic building block may be ineligible, but absence of complete preemption does not guarantee eligibility. Use the existing Steps 2A/2B analysis (and the streamlined analysis when appropriate) rather than using preemption as a separate test.

rubrics_metrics.name: Streamlined analysis for clearly non‑preemptive/self‑evident claims
rubrics_metrics.description: A streamlined analysis is available for claims that clearly do not seek to tie up any judicial exception such that others cannot practice it (i.e., claims with self‑evident eligibility).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The streamlined analysis yields the same result as the full Steps 2A/2B analysis for claims suitable for it. It is not a way to avoid the results of the full analysis; claims that require a full Step 2B significantly‑more inquiry are not suitable for the streamlined path. Examples 26 and 27 illustrate claims eligible under the streamlined analysis; Example 24 is not suitable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency and training for examiners applying the 2014 IEG
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure consistent eligibility analyses across the examining corps through guidance materials, comprehensive examples, training, and use of worksheets and answer keys.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance materials include the 2014 IEG, Quick Reference Sheet, Examples: Nature‑Based Products, Examples: Abstract Ideas, Appendix 1 examples, Appendix 2 index, and Appendix 3 case listings. Training (instructor‑led, workshops, videos, slides) was provided and materials (worksheets and sample rejections) are posted for examiner use to learn how to articulate prima facie rejections and apply Steps 2A/2B consistently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish generic computer implementation from invention that is 'significantly more'
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim that merely instructs to 'apply' an abstract idea on a computer or recites a computer performing generic functions is not sufficient to render an abstract idea eligible; conversely, claims in which generic computer components in combination perform non‑generic functions can be 'significantly more.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use case law and examples to determine whether the computer implementation is merely generic (e.g., Examples 7, 22, 24) or amounts to significantly more (e.g., Examples 3, 23, 25; DDR Holdings example discussed in case law). Analyze the claim as a whole and consider combinations of elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use case law precedent and illustrative examples to justify determinations
rubrics_metrics.description: When identifying exceptions and determining whether additional elements amount to significantly more, rely on comparisons to Supreme Court and Federal Circuit decisions and on illustrative examples indexed to considerations and subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appendix 1 and Appendix 2 provide new and previously issued examples mapped to judicial considerations; Appendix 3 lists selected cases with citations and subject matter. Examiners should refer to these resources and training materials (worksheets and answer keys) to support articulated reasoning in the record.
